$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big) \displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}\Big[{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big|{\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big)\Big] \displaystyle\;\;\;\;+\;\;{\rm Var}\Big({\mathbb{E}}\Big[\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big|{\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big]\Big) \displaystyle=p^{\ell}\;{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega})\Big|w\subseteq G_{\Omega}\Big)\;+\;p^{\ell}(1-p^{\ell})({\omega}-1)^{2s} \displaystyle\leq f(\ell,s)\Big(p^{\ell-1}({\omega}-\ell)^{2s-1}+({\omega}-\ell)p^{\ell+1-2s}\Big) \displaystyle\;\;\;\;+\;\;p^{\ell}(1-p^{\ell})({\omega}-1)^{2s} \displaystyle\leq f(\ell,s)\Big(p^{\ell-1}{{\omega}}^{2s-1}+{\omega}p^{\ell+1-2s}\Big)\;+\;p^{\ell}{{\omega}}^{2s}\,, $$

where the inequality follows from Equation (45). Similarly, for a walk $w$ with $\ell=1$ , and $s=k$ , we have,

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big)\leq f(k){{\omega}}^{2k-1}+g(k){\omega}p^{2-2k}+p{{\omega}}^{2k}\,, $$

where we used the inequality in (47).

For covariance term, we have,

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Cov}\Big(\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{1}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\,,\theta(w_{2},G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{2}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})\theta(w_{2},G_{\Omega})\Big|\mathbb{I}(w_{1}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{2}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big]p^{(\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}-\tilde{\ell})} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle f(\ell^{\prime},s^{\prime})p^{((\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}-\tilde{\ell})-(s_{1}+s_{2}))}\Big(({\omega}p)^{(s_{1}+s_{2})}+{\omega}p\Big)\,, $$

where the inequality follows from Equation (46).

### A.3 Proof of Lemma 3

When $G$ is a union of disjoint cliques, the estimator $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ defined in (21) has a compact representation. This follows from the fact that for any two nodes $i$ and $j$ that are connected in $G_{\Omega}$ , the neighborhoods of $i$ and $j$ in $G_{\Omega}$ exactly coincide. If this happens, then the estimator $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ simplifies as follows. Consider a walk $w$ with $s$ self-loops, $k$ edges (including self loops), and $\ell$ distinct nodes. Define a random integer $\widetilde{\tau}$ as the degree of a node in the clique that $w$ belongs to in the sampled graph $G_{\Omega}$ , conditioned on the fact that all nodes in $w$ are sampled (if a walk $w$ is sampled then it must belong to the same clique.). The randomness comes from the sampling of $\Omega$ . It is straightforward that $\widetilde{\tau}\sim{\rm Binom}({\omega}-\ell,p)+(\ell-1)$ as there are already $(\ell-1)$ neighbors from the walk $w$ and the rest of $(({\omega}-1)-(\ell-1))$ nodes are sampled in $\Omega$ with probability $p$ , where ${\omega}$ is the size of the clique in the original graph $G$ . For notational simplification, define a random integer $\tau\equiv\widetilde{\tau}-(\ell-1)$ that is distributed as $\tau\sim{\rm Binom}({\omega}-\ell,p)$ . In the example in Figure 8, for the walk $w=(1,2,2,2,3,3,1)$ , we have $\ell=3$ , $s=3$ , ${\omega}=7$ and a random instance of $\widetilde{\tau}=4$ that is $\tau=2$ . We claim that the estimator $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ given in (21) is a function of only $\tau$ , $\ell$ , $s$ and $p$ , and can be simplified as follows, and give a proof in Section A.4.

#### Lemma 4.

When the underlying $G$ is a union of disjoint cliques and $G_{\Omega}$ is a subgraph obtained via vertex sampling with a probability $p$ , for a length $k$ walk $w$ in $G_{\Omega}$ with $\ell$ distinct nodes and $s$ self-loops, we have

$$ \displaystyle\theta(w,G_{\Omega}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\langle A^{-1}_{s+1},\overline{\tau}\rangle\;, $$

where $\tau\equiv\widetilde{\tau}-(\ell-1)$ and $\widetilde{\tau}$ is the degree of any node in the clique that $w$ belongs to in the sampled graph $G_{\Omega}$ , $\overline{\tau}=[1,\tau,\tau^{2},\ldots,\tau^{s}]$ is a column vector of monomials of $\tau$ up to degree $s$ , and $A^{-1}_{s+1}$ is the $(s+1)$ -th row of the inverse of the matrix $A\in{\mathbb{R}}^{(s+1)\times(s+1)}$ satisfying $A\,\overline{{\omega}}\;\;=\;\;{\mathbb{E}}[\overline{\tau}]$ , for $\overline{{\omega}}=[1,({\omega}-1),({\omega}-1)^{2},\ldots,({\omega}-1)^{s}]$ , a column vector of monomials of $({\omega}-1)$ . Further, $A$ is a lower-triangular matrix that depends only on $\ell$ and $p$ , such that $\max_{i\in[s+1]}|(A^{-1})_{s+1,i}|=O(p^{-s})$ .

In the running example, $s=3$ , $\widetilde{\tau}=4$ , and $\ell=3$ , and therefore we have

$$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&0\\
p-\ell p&p&0&0\\
\ell^{2}p^{2}-\ell p^{2}-\ell p+p&-2\ell p^{2}+p^{2}+p&p^{2}&0\\
A_{41}&A_{42}&-3\ell p^{3}+3p^{3}&p^{3}\end{bmatrix}\;, $$

where $A_{41}=-\ell^{3}p^{3}+3\ell^{2}p^{2}+\ell p^{3}-3\ell p^{2}-\ell p+p$ and $A_{42}=3\ell^{2}p^{3}-6\ell p^{2}-p^{3}+3p^{2}+p$ . For any $s$ , corresponding $A$ can be computed immediately from the moments of a Binomial distribution up to degree $s$ . Since $\overline{{\omega}}={\mathbb{E}}[A^{-1}\overline{\tau}]$ , this representation immediately reveals that ${\mathbb{E}}[\theta(w,G_{\Omega})|w\subseteq G_{\Omega}]={\mathbb{E}}[\langle A_{s+1}^{-1},\overline{\tau}\rangle]=({\omega}-1)^{s}$ . Note that $\tau$ is conditioned on the event that all the nodes in $w$ are sampled.

With this definition, the variance of $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ can be upper bounded as follows. We will let $f(\ell,s)$ denote a function over $\ell$ and $s$ that captures the dependence in $\ell$ and $s$ that may change from line to line, and only track the dependence in ${\omega}$ and $p$ .

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega})\Big|w\subseteq G_{\Omega}\Big)\;\;\leq\;\;f(\ell,s)\max_{i\in[s+1]}{\rm Var}\big((A^{-1})_{s+1,i}\,\tau^{i-1}\big) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\leq\;f(\ell,s)\,p^{-2s}\,{\rm Var}(\tau^{s}) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\;f(\ell,s)p^{-2s}\Big({\mathbb{E}}[\tau^{2s}]-{\mathbb{E}}[\tau^{s}]^{2}\Big) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\leq\;f(\ell,s)p^{-2s}\Big(({\omega}-\ell)^{2s}p^{2s}+f(s)({\omega}-\ell)^{2s-1}p^{2s-1} \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\;\;\;\;+\;\;({\omega}-\ell)p-({\omega}-\ell)^{2s}p^{2s}\Big) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\leq\;f(\ell,s)\Big(p^{-1}({\omega}-\ell)^{2s-1}+({\omega}-\ell)p^{1-2s}\Big)\;, $$

where the first inequality follows from the fact that $\overline{\tau}$ is an $s+1$ dimensional vector, the second inequality follows from that fact that $\max_{i}|(A^{-1})_{s+1,i}|=O(p^{-s})$ from Lemma 4 and $\max_{i}={\rm Var}(\tau^{i-1})={\rm Var}(\tau^{s})$ , and in the third inequality we used the fact that $\tau\sim{\rm Binom}({\omega}-\ell,p)$ and a result from [3] that ${\mathbb{E}}[({\rm Binom}(d,p))^{s}]\leq\sum_{j=1}^{s}S(s,j)(dp)^{j}$ where $S(s,j)$ is the Sterling number of second kind. $S(s,s)=1$ , $S(s,1)=1$ and $S(s,j)\leq f(s)$ , for $2\leq j\leq s-1$ . We also used Jensen’s inequality ${\mathbb{E}}[({\rm Binom}(d,p))^{s}]\geq{\mathbb{E}}[({\rm Binom}(d,p))]^{s}$ . This proves the desired bound in (33).

To prove the bound in (47), observe that when $\ell=1$ , $\tau\sim{\rm Binom}({\omega}-1,p)$ , and we can tighten the above set of inequalities

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega})\Big|w\subseteq G_{\Omega}\Big)\;\;\leq\;\;g(k)\max_{i\in[k+1]}{\rm Var}\big((A^{-1})_{k+1,i}\,\tau^{i-1}\big) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\leq\;g(k)\,p^{-2k}\,{\rm Var}(\tau^{k}) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\;g(k)p^{-2k}\Big({\mathbb{E}}[\tau^{2k}]-{\mathbb{E}}[\tau^{k}]^{2}\Big) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\leq\;g(k)p^{-2k}\Big(({\omega}-1)^{2k}p^{2k}+f(k)({\omega}-1)^{2k-1}p^{2k-1} \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\;\;\;\;\;\;+\;\;({\omega}-1)p-({\omega}-1)^{2k}p^{2k}\Big) \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\leq\;f(k)p^{-1}({\omega}-1)^{2k-1}+g(k)({\omega}-1)p^{1-2k}\;. $$

For the covariance term, conditioned on the event that both the walks $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$ are observed, distribution of the random degree integer of each walk is $\tilde{\tau}_{1}=\tilde{\tau}_{2}=\tilde{\tau}_{12}$ , where $\tilde{\tau}_{12}\sim{\rm Binom}({\omega}-(\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}-\tilde{\ell}),p)+(\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}-\tilde{\ell}-1)$ . Therefore, the shifted Binomial random variable of each walk $\tau_{1}=\tilde{\tau}_{1}-(\ell_{1}-1)=\tilde{\tau}_{12}-(\ell_{1}-1)$ , and $\tau_{2}=\tilde{\tau}_{2}-(\ell_{2}-1)=\tilde{\tau}_{12}-(\ell_{2}-1)$ For the walk $w_{1}$ , with number of nodes $\ell_{1}$ , self loops $s_{1}$ , lets denote the matrix $A$ in (50) by $A_{1}$ , and similarly for walk $w_{2}$ , denote it by $A_{2}$ . Then we have,

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})\theta(w_{2},G_{\Omega})\Big|\mathbb{I}(w_{1}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{2}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big] \displaystyle\leq f(\ell^{\prime},s^{\prime})\max_{i_{1}\in[s_{1}+1],i_{2}\in[s_{2}+1]}{\mathbb{E}}\Big[(A_{1}^{-1})_{s_{1}+1,i_{1}}\,\tau_{1}^{i_{1}-1}(A_{2}^{-1})_{s_{2}+1,i_{2}}\,\tau_{2}^{i_{2}-1}\Big]\, \displaystyle\leq f(\ell^{\prime},s^{\prime})p^{-(s_{1}+s_{2})}{\mathbb{E}}\big[\tau_{1}^{s_{1}}\tau_{1}^{s_{2}}\big]\, \displaystyle\leq f(\ell^{\prime},s^{\prime})p^{-(s_{1}+s_{2})}\Big(({\omega}p)^{s_{1}+s_{2}}+{\omega}p\Big)\,, $$

where the first inequality follows from the fact that $\overline{\tau}_{1}$ is an $s_{1}+1$ dimensional vector, and $\overline{\tau}_{2}$ is an $s_{2}+1$ dimensional vector, the second inequality follows from that fact that $\max_{i}|(A_{1}^{-1})_{s_{1}+1,i_{1}}|=O(p^{-s_{1}})$ from Lemma 4 and $\max_{i_{1},i_{2}}={\mathbb{E}}[\tau_{1}^{i_{1}-1}\tau_{2}^{i_{2}-1}]={\mathbb{E}}[\tau_{1}^{s_{1}}\tau_{2}^{s_{2}}]$ , and in the third inequality we used a result from [3] that ${\mathbb{E}}[({\rm Binom}(d,p))^{s}]\leq\sum_{j=1}^{s}S(s,j)(dp)^{j}$ where $S(s,j)$ is the Sterling number of second kind. $S(s,j)\leq f(s)$ , for $1\leq j\leq s$ . This proves the desired bound in (46).

### A.4 Proof of Lemma 4

We are left to prove that the estimator $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ simplifies as in (50) when the original graph is a clique graph(or a union of disjoint cliques).

We use the notations introduced in Section 3 and Section A.3. Consider a closed walk $w$ of length $k$ on $\ell$ distinct nodes with $U=\{u_{1},\cdots,u_{\tilde{\ell}}\}$ set of nodes in it that have at least one self-loop, $|U|=\tilde{\ell}$ , and a total of $s$ self loops. If the underlying graph is a clique graph the partition of $V$ defined in (14), for any $T\subseteq U$ , is as follows:

$$ \displaystyle V_{T,U\setminus T}=\begin{cases}\emptyset&\text{if }|T|<|U|-1\\
d_{U,\emptyset}&\text{if }T=U\\
v&\text{if }T=U\setminus v,\text{ for any }v\in U\,.\end{cases} $$

Recall that $d_{U,\emptyset}\equiv\cap_{v\in U}\partial v$ . Therefore, we have,

$$ \displaystyle d_{T,U\setminus T}(w)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }|T|<|U|-1\\
\ell-\tilde{\ell}&\text{if }T=U\\
1&\text{if }T=U\setminus v,\text{ for any }v\in U\,.\end{cases} $$

If the underlying clique graph is of size ${\omega}$ then $|d_{U,\emptyset}|={\omega}-\tilde{\ell}$ . Using the fact $d_{T,U\setminus T}(\Omega)\sim{\rm Binom}(d_{T,U\setminus T}-d_{T,U\setminus T}(w),p)+d_{T,U\setminus T}(w)$ , as explained in Section 3, we have,

$$ \displaystyle d_{T,U\setminus T}(\Omega)\sim\begin{cases}0&\text{if }|T|<|U|-1\\
{\rm Binom}({\omega}-\ell,p)+(\ell-\tilde{\ell})&\text{if }T=U\\
1&\text{if }T=U\setminus v,\text{ for any }v\in U\,.\end{cases} $$

Using Equation (57) it is immediate that that degree of any node $u\in U$ is $d_{u}=d_{U,\emptyset}+(\tilde{\ell}-1)$ , and hence, ${\mathbb{E}}[\theta(w,G_{\Omega})|w\in G_{\Omega}]=\big(d_{U,\emptyset}+(\tilde{\ell}-1)\big)^{s}=({\omega}-1)^{s}$ . Therefore, an alternative characterization of the estimator defined in (21) is as following: $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ , conditioned on the event that all the nodes in the walk $w$ are sampled, is a random variable dependent only upon $d_{U,\emptyset}(\Omega)\sim{\rm Binom}({\omega}-\ell,p)+(\ell-\tilde{\ell})$ such that its conditional expectation is ${\mathbb{E}}[\theta(w,G_{\Omega})|w\in G_{\Omega}]=({\omega}-1)^{s}$ . With change of notations it is immediate that the estimator defined in (21) is same as the estimator in (50) when the underlying graph is a clique graph(or a disjoint union of cliques).

By the definition of $A$ , it follows that the diagonal entries are exactly ${\rm diag}([1,p,\ldots,p^{s}])$ and the bottom-left off-diagonal entris are all $\Theta(1)$ with respect to $p$ , and the top-right off-diagonal entries are all zeros. Applying the inverse to this lower triangular matrix, it follows that $A^{-1}$ is also a lower triangular matrix with diagonal entries ${\rm diag}([1,p^{-1},\ldots,p^{-s}])$ and the bottom-left off-diagonal entries are all $\Theta(1)$ . It follows that $\max_{i\in[s+1]}|(A^{-1})_{s+1,i}|=O(p^{-s})$ .

$$ \displaystyle\;{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big) \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\leq f(k){{d_{\rm max}}}^{2k-1}\;+\;g(k){d_{\rm max}}p^{2-2k}\;+\;p{{d_{\rm max}}}^{2k}\,, $$

and for any length- $k$ walks $w_{1},w_{2}$ over $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ distinct nodes with $\tilde{\ell}$ unique overlapping nodes, $|w_{1}\cap w_{2}|=\tilde{\ell}$ , $s_{1},s_{2}\geq 1$ self-loops respectively, the covariance term can be upper bounded by:

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Cov}\Big(\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{1}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\,,\theta(w_{2},G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{2}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big) \displaystyle\leq h(k)p^{((\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}-\tilde{\ell})-(s_{1}+s_{2}))}\Big(({d_{\rm max}}p)^{(s_{1}+s_{2})}+{d_{\rm max}}p\Big)\,, $$

for some function $h(k)=O(2^{k^{2}})$ , $f(k)=O(k!)$ , and $g(k)={\rm poly}(k)$ , where $p$ is the vertex sampling probabiliy.

The total count of length $k$ closed cycles on $\ell$ distinct nodes in a general graph on ${\omega}$ nodes graph with maximum degree ${d_{\rm max}}$ is bounded by $f(k){\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}$ . It follows from the observation that fixing a node in the cycle, there are at most ${d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}$ paths to $\ell-1$ -hop neighbors. That is $|w\in W:\mathcal{H}(w)\in\mathbb{H}_{k,\ell,s}|\leq f(k){\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}$ for any $1\leq s\leq k$ .

We use these inequalities to get bound on variance and covariance terms in (32).

For a walk $w\in W$ with $\mathcal{H}(w)\in\mathbb{H}_{k,\ell,s}$ with $1\leq s\leq k-2$ , using (60), we have,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{{\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}}{p^{2\ell}}{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big) \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\leq h(k)\Big(\frac{{{d_{\rm max}}}^{\ell+2s-1}}{p^{\ell}}+\frac{{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell}}{p^{\ell+2s-1}}\Big) \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\leq h(k){\omega}\Big(\frac{{d_{\rm max}}^{2k-3}}{p^{2}}+\frac{{d_{\rm max}}^{2}}{p^{2k-3}}\Big)\,. $$

For a walk $w\in W$ with $\mathcal{H}(w)\in\mathbb{H}_{k,\ell,s}$ with $\ell=1$ , $s=k$ , using (61), we have,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{{\omega}}{p^{2\ell}}{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big)\;\leq \displaystyle\;\;\;\;f(k){\omega}{{d_{\rm max}}}^{2k-1}p^{-2}\;+\;g(k){\omega}{d_{\rm max}}p^{-2k}\;+\;{\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{2k}p^{-1}\,. $$

For a walk $w$ with $s=0$ , $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})=1$ , and, we have,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{{\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}}{p^{2\ell}}{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{{\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}}{p^{\ell}}\,. $$

Combining, Equations (63), (64), and (65), and using $|w\in W:\mathcal{H}(w)\in\mathbb{H}_{k,\ell,s}|\leq f(k){\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{\ell-1}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\sum_{s=0}^{k-\ell+1}\sum_{H\in\mathbb{H}_{k,\ell,s}}\Big\{\frac{1}{p^{2\ell}}\,\sum_{w\in W:\mathcal{H}(w)=H}\mathbb{I}(w\subseteq G)\,\times \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega}){\mathbb{I}}(w\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big)\Big\} \displaystyle\leq h(k){\omega}{d_{\rm max}}p^{-2k}\;+\;{\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{2k}p^{-1}\,, $$

and if ${d_{\rm max}}p^{3}\leq 1/h(k)$ , then the above quantity is bounded by $g(k){\omega}{d_{\rm max}}p^{-2k}(1+o(1))$ . If ${d_{\rm max}}^{3}p\geq h(k)$ , then the above quantity is bounded by ${\omega}{d_{\rm max}}^{2k}p^{-1}(1+o(1))$ .

Analysis of covariance terms in (32) follows along the similar lines as that of the clique graph case and the result in Lemma 5 follows immediately.

### A.7 Proof of Lemma 6

We give a lemma similar to Lemma 3 for the case of a general graph that provides a bound on conditional variance and conditional covariance terms. We give a proof in Section A.8.

#### Lemma 7.

Under the hypothesis of Lemma 5, for length- $k$ walks $w_{1},w_{2}$ over $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ distinct nodes with $s_{1},s_{2}\geq 1$ self-loops respectively, the conditional variance of estimator $\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})$ , defined in (21), given that all the nodes in the walk are sampled can be upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})\Big|w_{1}\subseteq G_{\Omega}\Big)\;\;\leq\;\; \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\;h(k)\Big({d_{\rm max}}^{2s_{1}}+{d_{\rm max}}p^{1-2s_{1}}\Big)\;,\text{ and } \displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\theta(w_{1},G_{\Omega})\theta(w_{2},G_{\Omega})\Big|\mathbb{I}(w_{1}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\mathbb{I}(w_{2}\subseteq G_{\Omega})\Big]\;\;\leq \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\;h(k)p^{-(s_{1}+s_{2})}\Big(({d_{\rm max}}p)^{s_{1}+s_{2}}+{d_{\rm max}}p\Big)\;, $$

for some function $h(k)=O(2^{k^{2}})$ , where $p$ is the vertex sampling probability. Moreover, for a length $k$ walk $w$ with $\ell=1$ , and $s=k$ ,

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega})\Big|w\subseteq G_{\Omega}\Big)\leq f(k)p^{-1}{d_{\rm max}}^{2k-1}+g(k){d_{\rm max}}p^{1-2k}\,, $$

for some function $f(k)=O(k!)$ , and $g(k)={\rm poly}(k)$ .

Using the above lemma, proof of Lemma 6 follows along the lines of the proof of Lemma 2.

### A.8 Proof of Lemma 7

Recall that for a general graph $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ is an unbiased estimator of $\prod_{u\in w}d_{u}^{s_{u}}$ and is given in (21). It is easy to see that for any given walk $w$ on $\ell$ distinct nodes and with $s$ self-loops,

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\theta(w,G_{\Omega})|w\subseteq G_{\Omega}\Big)\leq h(k)\max_{\mathbb{T}}\Bigg\{{\rm Var}\bigg(\Big\{\prod_{T\in\mathbb{T}}\widehat{d}_{T,U\setminus T}^{(t_{T})}\Big\}\bigg)\Bigg\}\,, $$

where $h(k)=O(2^{k^{2}})$ . It follows from the fact that there are at most ${k/2}$ distinct nodes with self loops and hence at most $2^{k/2-1}$ partitions in (14) which leads to at most $2^{k^{2}/4}$ summation terms in (16). Further $\prod_{T\in\mathbb{T}}\widehat{d}_{T,U\setminus T}^{(t_{T})}$ is the product of independent random variables. Observe that using Lemma 3, we have

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}\Big(\widehat{d}_{T,U\setminus T}^{(t_{T})}\Big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle f(k)\Big(p^{-1}{d_{\rm max}}^{2t_{T}-1}+{d_{\rm max}}p^{1-2t_{T}}\Big)\, $$

and ${\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{d}_{T,U\setminus T}^{(t_{T})}]\leq{d_{\rm max}}^{t_{T}}$ . Using the fact that for independent random variables $X_{1},X_{2},\cdots,X_{n}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle{\rm Var}(X_{1}X_{2}\cdots X_{n})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Big({\rm Var}(X_{i})+({\mathbb{E}}[X_{i}])^{2}\Big)-\prod_{i=1}^{n}({\mathbb{E}}[X_{i}])^{2}\,, $$

we have,

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\mathbb{T}}\Bigg\{{\rm Var}\bigg(\Big\{\prod_{T\in\mathbb{T}}\widehat{d}_{T,U\setminus T}^{(t_{T})}\Big\}\bigg)\Bigg\} \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\leq\prod_{T\in\mathbb{T}}f(k)\Big(p^{-1}{d_{\rm max}}^{2t_{T}-1}+{d_{\rm max}}p^{1-2t_{T}}+{d_{\rm max}}^{2t_{T}}\Big) \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\leq f(k)\Big({d_{\rm max}}^{2s}+{d_{\rm max}}p^{1-2s}\Big)\, $$

where in the last inequality we used that $\sum_{T\in\mathbb{T}}t_{T}=s$ . (67) follows from collecting the above inequalities. (68) follows from the definition of $\theta(w,G_{\Omega})$ given in (21) and the proof of (46) of Lemma 3. (69) follows directly from (47) of Lemma 3.
